entities.summary:
Christ the Redeemer, an iconic statue of Jesus Christ, stands atop the Corcovado Mountain in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, symbolizing both faith and Brazilian culture. Completed in 1931, this colossal statue, designed by sculptor Paul Landowski and built by engineer Heitor da Silva Costa, has become a global representation of Christianity and a defining landmark of Rio, attracting millions of visitors each year. Its construction was a monumental effort, funded by donations from Brazilian Catholics and supported by the Brazilian government, reflecting the cultural and religious identity of Brazil in the early 20th century.

The statue was constructed between 1922 and 1931 and stands 30 meters tall, with an arm span of 28 meters, making it one of the largest statues of Jesus in the world. Its design was inspired by the Christ the Redeemer statue in the French town of Poitiers, with the aim of creating a symbol of peace and unity for the Brazilian people. The project was initiated during a period of increasing nationalism in Brazil, coinciding with the country's post-World War I growth and the rise of Catholicism as a unifying force in national identity. The statue's unveiling was attended by over 1,000 guests, including government officials and international dignitaries.

Over the decades, Christ the Redeemer has transcended its religious origins to become a cultural icon, inspiring countless representations in art, literature, and popular media. The statue was designated as one of the New Seven Wonders of the World in 2007, further cementing its status as a global symbol of faith and resilience. It has also become a focal point for social and political movements in Brazil, representing not only religious devotion but also national pride and unity in times of crisis.
